plan.contextChunk: This figure places two oblique triangles side by side in plain black outline, lettered identically, to contrast where the altitude lands. In each one the horizontal base is labeled b and runs from the vertex alpha at the left to the vertex gamma at the right, the apex is labeled beta, the short left side from alpha to beta is labeled c, and the long side sloping from beta down to gamma is labeled a. In the left triangle the apex sits above the interior of the base, and a dashed vertical altitude labeled h drops from beta to a point on b, meeting it at a small square marking the right angle; an arc at alpha marks the interior angle. In the right triangle the apex has shifted left beyond alpha, making the angle there obtuse, so the dashed altitude falls outside the figure and the base is carried leftward by a dashed extension to receive its foot. Two arcs appear at that lower left corner, one for the interior angle alpha and, immediately left of it, one for the angle alpha prime between side c and the extension. Setting the arrangements against each other shows that the same height construction serves both, provided the angle used is the one adjacent to the perpendicular, which supplies h for computing the area of a triangle with no right angle of its own.

interactionPlan.concept: For both acute and obtuse oblique triangles, the height is the perpendicular distance from the apex to the line containing the base, so an obtuse triangle may require using a base extension while preserving the same sine-height relationship.

demo_steps.title: Compare the two triangles
demo_steps.narration: Both the acute and obtuse constructions are visible at the same time. In the acute triangle, the altitude lands on the base segment; in the obtuse triangle, it lands outside the triangle on the line containing the base.

demo_steps.title: Focus on the height
demo_steps.narration: The highlighted dashed segments show that h is always measured perpendicular to the base line, not necessarily to a point inside the triangle.

demo_steps.title: Connect height to sine
demo_steps.narration: In the acute case, h comes directly from h = c sin(α). In the obtuse case, the small outside right triangle uses α′, and sin(α′) = sin(α), so the same height relationship still applies.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The height used in the area formula is always perpendicular to the line containing the base, so the same sine relationship works even when the altitude falls outside an obtuse triangle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw two clean black-outline geometry diagrams side by side on a white background, matching a textbook style. Do not add in-figure titles such as 'acute case' or 'obtuse case,' and do not use a pale yellow base highlight in the default view. The left panel should show an acute triangle with β above the interior of horizontal base b, and the dashed altitude h dropping to the base segment. The right panel should show an obtuse triangle with β to the left of α; draw the base segment b from α to γ and a dashed extension only from the altitude foot to α, not past the foot. Use small right-angle markers at both altitude feet. Keep all default lines black or gray, with optional blue emphasis only when the altitude relationship button is activated.

authoredContext:
Now that we can solve a triangle for missing values, we can use some of those values and the sine function to find the area of an oblique triangle. Recall that the area formula for a triangle is given as Area= 1 2 bh, where b is base and h is height. For oblique triangles, we must find h before we can use the area formula. Observing the two triangles in the figure, one acute and one obtuse, we can drop a perpendicular to represent the height and then apply the trigonometric property sinα= opposite hypotenuse to write an equation for area in oblique triangles. In the acute triangle, we have sinα= h c or csinα=h. However, in the obtuse triangle, we drop the perpendicular outside the triangle and extend the base b to form a right triangle. The angle used in calculation is α ′, or 180−α.

Two oblique triangles with standard labels. Both have a dotted altitude line h extended from angle beta to the horizontal base side b. In the first, which is an acute triangle, the altitude is within the triangle. In the second, which is an obtuse triangle, the altitude h is outside of the triangle.

demo_steps.title: Start with the acute arrangement
demo_steps.narration: Vertex β lies above the interior of base b, so the dashed altitude drops directly onto the base segment. The angle at α and side c form a right triangle whose vertical leg is h.

demo_steps.title: Construct the altitude
demo_steps.narration: Click side b to drop the perpendicular from β. The right-angle marker shows that h is measured at 90 degrees to the base line, giving the height needed for the area formula.

demo_steps.title: Move β across α
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider left so β passes beyond α. The foot of the perpendicular can no longer land on the base segment, so the base line must be extended.

demo_steps.title: Read the obtuse construction
demo_steps.narration: In the obtuse view, the dashed extension and angle alpha prime appear. The same perpendicular height h is still used, but it is supplied by the small adjacent right triangle outside the original triangle.

plan.keyInsight: The altitude of a triangle is always perpendicular to the line containing the base, so in an obtuse triangle the height may be constructed outside the triangle.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean black-outline geometry diagram on a white background. Place α at the left end of a horizontal base and γ at the right end, with β movable horizontally above the base line. Label the base b, the left side c, and the long right side a in italic math style. In acute view, β is above a point between α and γ and the dashed altitude h falls inside the triangle. In obtuse view, β is shifted left of α, the base continues left as a dashed extension, and the altitude falls to that extension; show both α and the adjacent α′ arc near the lower-left corner. Keep the right-angle square small and clear, and make the altitude dashed so it reads as an auxiliary construction rather than a triangle side.

discrepancies: The source figure is a side-by-side comparison of acute and obtuse cases, while the generated default view shows only the acute case and hides the obtuse construction behind controls/steps.
The generated drawing adds an 'acute case' title and a pale yellow highlighted base interaction strip that are not present in the black-and-white textbook figure.
In the obtuse state, the dashed base extension is coded to extend noticeably past the altitude foot to the left, whereas the source primarily shows the extension segment from the foot to α.
